title: Wendelin and Ursinus make every voluntary act free, so that God is freely good because not by compulsion
source_text: VIII. Quamvis igitur ille, & qui cum eo sentiunt, agnoscant discrimen esse inter actus voluntatis, nempe ad quosdam voluntatem determinatam esse, aliorum vero respectu natura sua manere idoneam ad opposita; censent tamen voluntatem, tam horum quam illorum respectu, liberam dici debere, & tam hos quam illos libere a voluntate prodire & elici. Ac proinde distinguunt quidem inter voluntarium simpliciter, & illud quod fit ex electione: sed inter voluntarium & liberum non distinguunt. Nam utrumque volunt aeque late patere, & quicquid voluntarium est, hoc ipso esse liberum. Nec ullam necessitatem quae voluntarii naturam non evertat, libertatis naturam evertere existimant. Adeoque quamvis Deus per naturam bonus sit, docent tamen illum esse libere bonum, quoniam non coacte, sed voluntarie bonus est. Sicuti videre est apud Zachariam Ursinum loco jam allegato. Liberum, inquit, vocatur ἑκούσιον, hoc est, spontaneum: quod opponitur ἀκουσίῳ, hoc est, involuntario, & coacto: non autem ἀναγκαίῳ, seu necessario. Potest enim ἑκούσιον consistere cum ἀναγκαίῳ, sed non cum ἀκουσίῳ, ut Deus & sancti Angeli ἀναγκαίως, hoc est, necessario sunt boni: non tamen ἀκουσίως, hoc est, coacte, sed liberrime: quia principium suae bonitatis habent in seipsis, liberam voluntatem.
pass_a_gloss: Although therefore he, and those who agree with him, acknowledge that there is a difference between acts of the will, namely that to some the will is determined, but in respect of others it remains by its nature apt for opposites; they nevertheless judge that the will, as much in respect of these as of those, ought to be called free, and that as well these as those proceed and are elicited freely from the will. And therefore they distinguish indeed between the voluntary simply, and that which is done from election: but between the voluntary and the free they do not distinguish. For they will both to extend equally widely, and whatever is voluntary, by this very fact to be free. Nor do they think that any necessity which does not overturn the nature of the voluntary, overturns the nature of liberty. And so although God is good by nature, they teach yet that he is freely good, since he is good not by coaction, but voluntarily. As may be seen in Zacharias Ursinus in the place already alleged. Free, he says, is called hekousion, that is, spontaneous: which is opposed to akousion, that is, involuntary, and coerced: but not to anankaion, or necessary. For hekousion can stand with anankaion, but not with akousion, as God and the holy Angels are anankaios, that is, necessarily good: yet not akousios, that is, by coaction, but most freely: because they have the principle of their goodness in themselves, a free will.
pass_b_english: He and those who agree with him admit a difference among the will's acts: the will is fixed on some of them, while toward others it stays by nature able to go either way. Still they hold that the will should be called free with respect to both kinds, and that both kinds come freely from the will.

So they do distinguish between what is simply voluntary and what comes from choice, but they draw no line between the voluntary and the free. They want the two to cover the same ground, so that whatever is voluntary is free for that very reason. They do not think any necessity destroys the nature of freedom unless it also destroys the nature of the voluntary.

They therefore teach that God, though good by nature, is freely good, because his goodness is not forced but willed. Ursinus says this in the passage cited above: "What is free is called hekousion, that is, spontaneous. It is the opposite of akousion, the involuntary and forced, but not of anankaion, the necessary.

"Hekousion can go with anankaion, but not with akousion. God and the holy angels are good anankaios, that is, necessarily, yet not akousios, that is, under force; they are good most freely, because the source of their goodness is in themselves, a free will."

choices.why: Electio in this locus is the act of choosing after deliberation (Aristotle's prohairesis); 'choice' keeps it parallel with 'free choice'.
